bodyText:
Contributing guidelines

 I have read CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md

Module(s)
mini.test
Question
I've installed mini.test on its own, and due to the plugin not having a plugin/mini.test/test.lua (or similar) directory, it does not trigger a SourcePost event. Any idea how I would fix this?

comment_data.body:
That's expected, and there's nothing to fix in mini.test. `SourcePost` fires once per file that gets sourced, and `:packadd` only sources the plugin's `plugin/` and `ftdetect/` scripts. The standalone mini.test repo only has `lua/` and `doc/`, so `:packadd mini.test` adds it to `runtimepath` and sources nothing, hence no event. You'd see the same with any Lua-only plugin.

Quick check with a Lua-only plugin next to one that has a `plugin/` file (Nvim 0.12):

```
after packadd mini.test: SourcePost hits={} rtp_has=true require_ok=true
after packadd withplugin: SourcePost hits={ "withplugin.lua" }
```

`:packadd` is synchronous though, so you don't need an event. Whatever you were hooking on `SourcePost` can just go right after it:

```lua
vim.cmd.packadd("mini.test")
require("mini.test").setup()
```

If you install it with `vim.pack.add()`, its `load` option can take a function that gets the plugin data, and then you're in charge of loading:

```lua
vim.pack.add({ "https://github.com/nvim-mini/mini.test" }, {
  load = function(p)
    vim.cmd.packadd(p.spec.name)
    require("mini.test").setup()
  end,
})
```

See `:h :packadd` and `:h vim.pack.add()`.

I'm not sure if the second part of your reply is useful for my problem, but I'll elaborate on what I mean and why I need it. Apologies if I misunderstood.

An example of what I'm talking about is executing a setup on `:packadd` which I've pasted below for plugin `foo`. I don't need mini.test to be loaded every time I open Neovim. I understand the argument of "it doesn't have that much overhead", but it's not my point here since I want to have control what gets loaded and when.

```lua
-- Plugin foo is 'on-demand' and won't be loaded until :packadd
vim.pack.add({"repo/for/foo.nvim"}, {
    load = function() end
})

-- Load setups on :packadd
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("SourcePost", {
    group = config_augroup,
    callback = function(ev)
        local pluginname = vim.fs.basename(ev.file)

        if pluginname == 'foo.lua' and not package.loaded['foo'] then
            require("foo").setup()
        end
    end
})
```

Is my above example similar to what you were referring to? I hope I explained it well enough. This method works for plugins who have `plugin/foo/foo.lua`, as you've also mentioned.

reply_data.body:
Got it, you want it on demand, not loaded at startup. Then there's no event to hook, unfortunately. `:packadd mini.test` only adds the directory to `runtimepath`, and since the plugin has no `plugin/` file nothing is sourced, so `SourcePost` never fires for it. I also checked `SourcePre` and `OptionSet` on `runtimepath`: neither fires on `:packadd` either.

What works is doing the `:packadd` yourself through a small command, so you still decide when it loads and the setup runs right after:

```lua
local setups = {
  ["mini.test"] = function() require("mini.test").setup() end,
}

vim.api.nvim_create_user_command("Packadd", function(opts)
  vim.cmd.packadd(opts.args)
  local setup = setups[opts.args]
  if setup then setup() end
end, { nargs = 1, complete = "packadd" })
```

Then `:Packadd mini.test` loads it and runs its setup (with the real mini.test, `MiniTest` exists right after), and tab completion still lists your opt packages. Plugins that aren't in the table just get a plain `:packadd`, so you can use it for everything and keep your `SourcePost` approach for the ones that have a `plugin/` file.

comment_data.body:
> I've installed mini.test on its own, and due to the plugin not having a plugin/mini.test/test.lua (or similar) directory, it does not trigger a SourcePost event. Any idea how I would fix this?

The answer to this *particular* question is "The fix depends on what you try to achieve. This behavior is expected, precisely because of what you described". There is no need in 'plugin/mini-test.lua' in standalone repo, since they are all designed to be merely a copy of 'mini.nvim' parts with all their suggested workflows.

> An example of what I'm talking about is executing a setup on `:packadd` which I've pasted below for plugin `foo`. I don't need mini.test to be loaded every time I open Neovim. I understand the argument of "it doesn't have that much overhead", but it's not my point here since I want to have control what gets loaded and when.

Depends on what you mean by "to be loaded". Usually the problem here is wanting to delay sourcing `plugin/*` files since this introduces side effects (mappings, user commands, autocommands, highlight groups). If not doing that is enough to qualify as "to not be loaded", then executing `:packadd` during startup is fine (since there are `plugin/*`).

My personal preference and recommendation is to not do `SourcePost` approach, since it is not quite reliable (as this question reveals). The "two stage" loading "now and later" type is usually good enough for most configs. Like it is [done in MiniMax](https://nvim-mini.org/MiniMax/configs/nvim-0.12/#init.lua), for example.

If you want to completely avoid increasing 'runtimepath' completely, then doing two steps (`:packadd` + `:lua require('mini.test').setup()`) manually or via some helper command is the way to go.

Finally, the solution for 'mini.test' specific case:
- It doesn't *really* need the `require('mini.test').setup()` for the correct operation. Skipping it will not create default highlight groups and global `_G.MiniTest`, which might be fine.
- Use 'mini.nvim' directly. If you use at least one other module, then it would add less 'runtimepath' overhead.

Hope this helps.

Since standalone 'mini.test' doesn't have plugin scripts, doing :packadd mini.test will only modify 'runtimepath'. If this is not the problem for you, then using plain vim.pack.add during startup (without load = function() end) should be fine.
To perform side effects later, execute :lua require('mini.test').setup(). Although they are not a hard requirement for 'mini.test'.
